section 1.2: pleistocene climate and sea level fluctuation
content: 1.2 pleistocene climate and sea level fluctuation global climate fluctuation during the pleistocene (c. 2.6–0.01 ma) have drive multiple cycle of eustatic (or worldwide) sea level change, with several of the most recent cycle exceed 100 m vertical change from minimum to maximum sea stand. during warm interglacial period, elevated sea level slow river discharge to the sea, allow sediment to settle out and build up floodplain. during cool glacial period, lower sea level allow river to incise more deeply into their sediment bed as they approach their mouth, erode floodplain and steepen the river gradient. this repeat formation and erosion of amazonian whitewater floodplain (i.e., várzeas) during sea level high and low stand be refer to as the irion cycle (irion and kalliola 2010).

content: 5.2.2.2 pdo, amo, mjo in addition to enso, there be two other mode of interannual and interdecadal variability with teleconnection that influence the climate of the amazon, the pacific decadal oscillation (pdo) and the atlantic multidecadal oscillation (amo). they represent change in the organization of air-sea interaction that vary at decadal scale and affect the sea surface, induce later circulation and rainfall change in the amazon. for a detailed definition of these mode of variability, please see the glossary. consistent with the enso (en) positive phase, the pdo and amo's positive phase match the intensification of negative rainfall anomaly in the amazon towards the end of 2015, during the 2015-16 en event (aragão et al. 2018). this finding be consistent with previous work (kayano and capistrano, 2014) show that the atlantic multidecadal oscillation (amo) and enso influence south american rainfall at the end of the year, before the peak of en.

section 5.3.6.1: severe storm, blowdown, and impact on forest ecosystem dynamic wind be a major cause of disturba
content: 5.3.6.1 severe storm, blowdown, and impact on forest ecosystem dynamic wind be a major cause of disturbance in forest worldwide, with impact range from minor loss of leaf to widespread tree-mortality (mitchell 2013). in the amazon, convective storm can generate strong downdraft wind and extreme rainfall (e.g., 26-41 m s-1 and 30 mm h-1, respectively) (garstang et al. 1998; fujita et al. 1990; negrón-juárez et al. 2010) that can fell forest patch range in size from <2 ha (negrón-juárez et al. 2011) to >3,000 ha (nelson et al. 1994). large blowdown can be associate with squall line (negrón-juárez et al. 2010; araujo et al. 2017). forest blowdown can be detect with remote sense imagery because they create a large contrast in geometric and reflectance pattern between image acquire before and after the event (figure 5.6a).

document:
chapter: sustainable development goal (sdgs) and the amazon
section 26.3: conclusion
content: 26.3 conclusion the devil be in the detail. just as the 2030 agenda highlight complementarity between different sustainable development objective, progress in the implementation of one objective can lead to negative impact on another (katila et al. 2019). at the amazon present, policy to address hunger, access to energy, job creation, economic growth, and infrastructure can fulfill sdg target while have a catastrophic impact on the amazon’s natural capital and, as a result, on the sustainability of these investment. in fact, the big threat to a resilient future in the amazon include lowland dams, which be count as contribute to the provision of affordable and clean energy (sdg 7); and road infrastructure (sdg 8) which fuel agricultural expansion (sdg 2). similarly, there can be trade-off or synergy between life on land (sdg 15) and decent work and economic growth (sdg 8).

content: 23.3.1 surface albedo and radiation balance deforestation to expand agriculture result in permanent change to the surface radiation balance, impact climate at local and regional scale. crop and pasture that typically replace forest have shallow root system and a seasonal grow season, which tend to decrease the net surface radiation (rnet), which be the sum of solar shortwave and net longwave radiation ﬂuxe absorb by the land surface (coe et al. 2016). rnet reduction be link to increase in the surface albedo and the outcome flux of longwave radiation, limit the system’s capacity to cycle water through evapotranspiration. these local change in the rnet and water balance alter circulation and shorten the rainy season (butt et al. 2011; knox et al. 2011), affect crop productivity over the agricultural frontier over the amazon and cerrado region.

content: 1.2 pleistocene climate and sea level fluctuation global climate fluctuation during the pleistocene (c. 2.6–0.01 ma) have drive multiple cycle of eustatic (or worldwide) sea level change, with several of the most recent cycle exceed 100 m vertical change from minimum to maximum sea stand. during warm interglacial period, elevated sea level slow river discharge to the sea, allow sediment to settle out and build up floodplain. during cool glacial period, lower sea level allow river to incise more deeply into their sediment bed as they approach their mouth, erode floodplain and steepen the river gradient. this repeat formation and erosion of amazonian whitewater floodplain (i.e., várzeas) during sea level high and low stand be refer to as the irion cycle (irion and kalliola 2010).

content: 18.2.1 driver of deforestation and extractivist development project in the colombian amazon deforestation in the amazon region do not follow a shared logic. instead, the diversity of the region correspond to the heterogeneity of the dynamic of deforestation and thus require locally or regionally adapt protection strategy. the main driver for deforestation include: i) cattle ranch; ii) land grab; iii) extractivism; iv) illicit drug cultivation; v) infrastructure development; and vi) the expansion of the agricultural frontier by smallholder (see chapter 19 and 20). however, the various driver of deforestation should not be consider as equivalently relevant for deforestation, nor should they be analyze in isolation, but rather in their interdependence (hoffmann, garcía márquez and krueger 2018).

content: the conservation paradigm have not be strong enough to control or detain the main adverse environmental and social impact of the extractive development model. as a result, unsustainable extractivism remain the lead paradigm guide public policy and private investment. the brazilian case highlight complex politic link to the ‘epochal process’ of hegemonic and counterhegemonic movement. on the one hand, the challenge pose by environmentalism to the extractive development hegemony provoke strong reaction in the latter’s advocate, reverse many of the advance make in the 2000s (section 17.4). on the other hand, the subjugation of environmental policy by these hegemonic process jeopardize its resilience to change in the natural environment (e.g., lovejoy and nobre 2017) or broad geopolitical and economic preference (section 17.4). a middle ground need to be find.

content: uplifting of air by the ande. land surface process partition precipitation into evapotranspiration (~1,220 mm per year), surface runoff, and deep drainage to the groundwater. the amazon river system drain the surface and groundwater component of this abundant rainfall, form the world’s large watershed and feed the world’s large river, with a mean discharge of 220,000 m3/s. the amazon have a discharge five time large than the congo, the world’s second-large river. the flow be highly seasonal, and imbalance between the addition of water to river by rainfall and the rate of water export downstream cause seasonal flooding over a large floodplain area, with beneficial ecological and biogeochemical implication. extreme flood and drought event be associate with intense interannual rainfall variability, which, in turn, influence forest fire and biogeochemical cycle. keyword: amazon water balance, extreme event

content: 1.2.3 set the stage: pangea breakup and birth of the ande the tectonic separation of south america and africa lead to the opening of the south and equatorial atlantic ocean. this separation and the eventual uplift of the ande along the western margin of south america fundamentally alter the geological, geomorphological, and climatic condition of the entire continent, and lead to the current geographic configuration (figure. 1.3 and fig. 1.4). the breakup of pangea eventually transform this supercontinent into multiple small continent, include south america, africa, and the indian subcontinent, with antarctica and australia break away from south america around 45 ma (seton et al. 2012). this paleogeographic rearrangement create new continental margin and large-scale drainage readjustment.

chapter: the physical hydroclimate system of the amazon

content: fire disturbance have an important ecological effect on the vegetation structure and composition due to influence on the ecological and biogeochemical process of vegetation directly affect the net primary production and respiration that, over time, lead to change in composition and structure of vegetation (alve et al. 1997). fire change plant' phenology and physiology, modify competition among tree, and lower canopy plant such as grass, shrub, and liana. depend on its frequency and intensity, fire may increase tree' mortality and transform an undisturbed forest into a disturbed and flammable one (house et al. 2003; hirota et al. 2010; hoffmann et al. 2012). tree specie associate with forest or savanna vegetation differ in numerous physiological characteristic, such as fire survivorship (hoffmann et al. 2009; ratnam et al. 2011) and their wood and foliar characteristic (gotsch et al. 2010).

content: evidence from paleorecord that cover the last two glacial-interglacial cycle (c. 250,000 year) reveal distinct climate profile in the eastern and western amazon, the so-call south american precipitation dipole (cheng et al. 2013). this dipole consist of a differential precipitation pattern over the amazon, where wet-dry condition vary substantially in the eastern amazon, while precipitation variability be much less in the western amazon, include the ande (cheng et al. 2013; baker and fritz 2015, wang et al. 2017). the effect of this precipitation dipole on biotic landscape be poorly know, as fossil pollen sequence in the lowland amazon often lack time series old than 50,000 yr (flantua et al. 2015). however, record cover the last glacial period around c. 21 ka show different specie composition and structure of lowland and andean forest when compare to the present (mayle et al. 2009), without necessarily a shift between biome (häggi et al. 2017).

section 20.7: deforestation
content: 20.7 deforestation deforestation be a driver of aquatic degradation that can have effect that differ between the directly impact area and area downstream; local deforestation can have regional consequence. at the small to medium scale, deforestation usually result in increase runoff and discharge; for example, deforestation result in a 25% increase in discharge in large river system such as the tocantin and araguaia river, with little change in precipitation (coe et al. 2009). at a large scale, atmospheric feedback (reduce precipitation cause by decrease evapotranspiration) can change the water balance, not only in the basin where deforestation have occur but throughout the entire amazon via atmospheric circulation (coe et al. 2009).

content: the forest's fundamental role in regional moisture transport and balance have be discuss in the context of the biotic pump theory. this theory suggest that atmospheric condensation of water vapor supply by plant transpiration from forest be a mechanism that not only contribute to recycling of rain (as describe in section 7.2.1 above), but also exert a major influence over atmospheric dynamic (makarieva and gorshkov, 2007; makarieva et al. 2013). specifically, re-condensation of the forest’s evapotranspire water be a mass removal of water from the gas phase that induce a decline in air pressure in the lower atmosphere, with consequent horizontal pressure gradient that accelerate air motion. et-supply water vapor thus provide a store of potential energy available to drive additional wind (beyond what would be expect from the general atmospheric circulation) that then contribute to the transport of ocean-evaporate water vapor to continental forest.

content: amazon fishery be highly seasonal, and fishing activity be relate to the seasonal rise and fall of the amazon river (junk et al. 1989). along the main channel of the amazon, high water occur between may and june and low water in october-november. three main group of fish can be distinguish. long-distance migratory catfish, several of which travel across the basin, spawn in andean headwater and pass their juvenile phase in the amazon estuary (barthem and goulde 1997; duponchelle et al. 2021). a second group of middle-distance migratory specie, of which the characidae be the most important, move in and out of the floodplain over their life cycle, feed in flood forest during the highwater season. the third group consist of sedentary specie, such as the highly prize pirarucu or paiche (arapaima spp.) that spend much of their lifecycle in floodplain lake (barthem and goulde 2007; see chapter 30).

section 7: general content
content: the warm and humid climate that sustain amazonian rainforest be partly a consequence of interaction between the forest and the atmosphere. this chapter assess the biogeophysical process by which the rainforest provide moisture and energy to maintain its own climate. a combination of several plant trait and process – low albedo, rough canopy, deep rooting, plant hydraulic lift, and biological regulation of water flux through leaf – allow the capture of water store at deep soil layer. these mechanism provide a steady flow of water vapor into the atmosphere, which be recycle internally in the amazon and be a major water vapor source to other south american region. regionally average, about 28% of the rainfall in the amazon have fall at least once, with this fraction increase westward, until it exceed 50% at the foot of the ande. the rainforest also play an important climate regulation role in the southern amazon during the dry-to-wet season transition

chapter: opportunity and challenge for a healthy standing forest and flow river bioeconomy in the amazon
section 30.4.2: non-timber forest product
content: the work of research institution on expand knowledge and improve diversified system be essential. agronomic research show that system be just as important as cultivar and, in a region such as the amazon, the combination of scientific and traditional method be especially important. rather than produce a single commodity with high acceptance and market value, system base on an immense variety of plant can have higher yield and return. an interesting example be that of the oiapoque indigenous community. they produce açaí (with embrapa’s support) use good practice, such as enrich their garden with high-agronomic quality, pest-free banana and citrus seedling. the result be an increase in production and supply to urban population, both at market and by direct sale, of diversified indigenous product (flour, gum, tapioca, pepper, tucupi, chicory, manioc, banana, cane, piquiá, lime, tucumã, cupuaçu, taperabá), in addition to açaí.

chapter: restoration option for the amazon
section 28.5: indicator of success
content: there be a broad range of potential indicator of success (e.g. ruiz-jaen and mitchell aide, 2005; stanturf et al., 2015), and they vary greatly in their ease and scalability. for example, open-source platform such as mapbiomas mean that year-onyear change in forest cover can be assess across the amazon with reasonable accuracy. however, property-level or landscapeand catchment-specific change will likely require more tailor assessment and higher-resolution imagery (d. r. a. de almeida et al., 2020). this be especially important when restoration focusse on narrow strip or small patch, include riparian zone; buffer the edge of exist forest; develop agroforestry system rather than closed-canopy forest; or focusse on aquatic system, non-forest ecosystem or fauna.

section 2.3: evolution of amazonian forest
content: in the miocene, uplift of the northern ande lead to a profound reorganization of the river network and the formation of the pebas mega-wetland, a system (hoorn et al. 1995, 2010, 2017; albert et al. 2018), of vast lacustrine and swampy environment in the western amazon (hoorn 1993; wesselingh and salo 2006). progressive uplift of the northern ande also affect the regional climate, lead to increase precipitation due to the orography (poulsen et al. 2010). vast area of flooded forest be then establish, compose of palm (i.e., grimsdalea), fern, and poaceae, among other (hoorn 1994; jaramillo et al. 2017; hoorn et al. 2017; kirschner and hoorn 2020). in addition, marine incursion into the western amazon allow estuarine taxa to colonize the pebas shore (hoorn 1993; boonstra et al. 2015; jaramillo et al. 2017).

section 16.1: protect area downgrade, downsize, and degazettement (paddd) (cont.)
content: in ecuador paddd event, as analyze by lópez-acevedo (2015), have be mostly characterize by the reconfiguration of limit with the aim to exclude extractive area from protect area (pas). as a result, the extent of the affected protect area (pas) end up be large, though not necessarily a well fit for conservation. there have also be elimination of protect forest to allow for mining concession. accord to the environmental code in force, “if necessary and consider the result of such technical evaluation, the national environmental authority may re-delimit they [the protect area] or change their category under technical consideration, as appropriate.” this leave rather open the legal procedure for any paddd event, especially in term of the discretionary decision by the environmental authority.
